The update is A-stable when the closed left half-plane $\{z:\operatorname{Re}z\le0\}$ is contained in $\mathcal S_R$. A rational one-step update is L-stable when it is A-stable and

$$\lim_{\substack{|z|\to\infty\\ \operatorname{Re}z\le0}}R(z)=0,$$

where the limit means that the values tend to zero along every sequence in the closed left half-plane whose modulus tends to infinity.

$$\pi_z(\zeta)=\rho(\zeta)-z\sigma(\zeta).$$

The multistep absolute-stability region consists of those $z$ for which the leading coefficient $\alpha_k-z\beta_k$ is nonzero and every root of $\pi_z$ satisfies the root condition: all roots have modulus at most one, and every root of modulus one is simple. citations.quote:
Input a vector field $f(t,y)$, a finite grid $t_0,\ldots,t_N$, starting states $Y_0,Y_1\in\mathbb R^d$ (so $N\ge1$), and for each later step a prescribed closed ball $B_{n+1}\subset\mathbb R^d$ that specifies the admissible implicit branch. Before any evaluation, if either starting state has dimension different from $d$, return `invalid-input`; otherwise, if any time increment is nonpositive, return `invalid-grid`. Set $h_n=t_{n+1}-t_n$ and $r_n=h_n/h_{n-1}$ for $1\le n<N$.

For $n=1,\ldots,N-1$, form the equation

$$\frac{(1+2r_n)Z-(1+r_n)^2Y_n+r_n^2Y_{n-1}}{h_n(1+r_n)}=f(t_{n+1},Z).$$

If this equation has exactly one root $Z$ in $B_{n+1}$, set $Y_{n+1}=Z$ and continue. If it has no root there, return `no-root` with the computed prefix; if it has more than one root there, return `ambiguous-branch` with the computed prefix. If an evaluation of $f$ is undefined, return `evaluation-failure` with the prefix. On reaching $N$, return `completed` and $(Y_0,\ldots,Y_N)$. The procedure is defined for arbitrary positive adjacent step ratios; no convergence or accuracy property is part of this algorithm.

The coefficients are those obtained from the quadratic interpolation derivative in [[lem-variable-step-bdf2-interpolation-and-local-defect]]. A separate theorem gives the uniform ratio hypotheses needed for second-order convergence; they are not part of this algorithm.

Let $k\ge1$, $d\ge1$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be the right-hand side of a first-order initial-value problem on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, using the convention of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **constant-step $k$-step linear multistep method** has real coefficients $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_k,\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k\ne0$ and advances values by

$$\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jY_{n+j}=h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j f(t_{n+j},Y_{n+j}),\qquad t_{n+j}=t_n+jh,\quad h>0.$$

Multiplying all coefficients by the same nonzero scalar leaves the method unchanged; one may normalize $\alpha_k=1$. Its **characteristic polynomials** are

$$\rho(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_j\zeta^j,\qquad \sigma(\zeta)=\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_j\zeta^j.$$

For an exact solution $y$, the **unscaled local residual** at $t_n$ is

$$\tau_n(h;y)=\sum_{j=0}^k\alpha_jy(t_n+jh)-h\sum_{j=0}^k\beta_jy'(t_n+jh).$$

The method has **order at least $p$**, where $p\ge1$ is an integer, if, for every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$, every right-hand side $f:U\to\mathbb R^d$ as above, and every exact solution $y$ of that IVP with $p+1$ continuous derivatives, $\tau_n(h;y)=O(h^{p+1})$ uniformly for admitted starting times in every fixed compact interval on which the indicated derivatives are bounded. It is **consistent** if it has order at least one. Equivalently, with the above coefficient convention, consistency is $\rho(1)=0$ and $\rho'(1)=\sigma(1)$.

The **root condition** is that every complex root of $\rho$ has modulus at most one and every root of modulus one has algebraic multiplicity one. The method is **zero-stable** if for each $T>0$ there is a constant $M_T$ independent of $N$ such that every solution of the homogeneous recurrence $\sum_j\alpha_jY_{n+j}=0$ on the uniform grid $h=T/N$ satisfies

$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|Y_n\|_\infty\le M_T\max_{0\le j<k}\|Y_j\|_\infty.$$

Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_{0\le i<d}|x_i|$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The root-condition equivalence for zero-stability is established separately.

For the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, a step size $h>0$ gives $z=h\lambda$. A one-step scalar update has stability function $R$ when one step sends $y_n$ to $y_{n+1}=R(z)y_n$. If $R$ is rational, write it in reduced form; it is defined at $z$ exactly when its denominator is nonzero there. Its absolute-stability region is

$$\mathcal S_R=\{z\in\mathbb C:R(z)\text{ is defined and }|R(z)|\le1\}.$$

The update is A-stable when the closed left half-plane $\{z:\operatorname{Re}z\le0\}$ is contained in $\mathcal S_R$. A rational one-step update is L-stable when it is A-stable and

$$\lim_{\substack{|z|\to\infty\\ \operatorname{Re}z\le0}}R(z)=0,$$

where the limit means that the values tend to zero along every sequence in the closed left half-plane whose modulus tends to infinity.

For a linear multistep method with the coefficient and polynomial convention of [[def-linear-multistep-method-consistency-order-and-root-condition]], substitution of the scalar test equation gives the characteristic polynomial

$$\pi_z(\zeta)=\rho(\zeta)-z\sigma(\zeta).$$

The multistep absolute-stability region consists of those $z$ for which the leading coefficient $\alpha_k-z\beta_k$ is nonzero and every root of $\pi_z$ satisfies the root condition: all roots have modulus at most one, and every root of modulus one is simple. This criterion concerns constant-step scalar test recurrences.

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For every real $r$, write $\lambda_r$ for its canonical image in $\mathbb C$. Then
$$
|\lambda_r|_{\mathbb C}=|r|_{\mathbb R}.
$$

derivations.claim: Setting $r_n=1$ in [F1] gives $3Y_{n+1}-4Y_n+Y_{n-1}=2h f(t_{n+1},Y_{n+1})$. Substituting $f(t,y)=\lambda y$ and a trial mode $Y_n=\zeta^n$, the polynomial convention in [F2] gives $(3-2z)\zeta^2-4\zeta+1=0$.

The constant term is one, so $\zeta\ne0$. Put $w=1/\zeta$, $a=\operatorname{Re}w$, and $r=|w|$. By [F4] and [F5], $1=|1|=|\zeta w|=|\zeta||w|$, so $r=1/|\zeta|$. Solving the equation in step 1.1 for $z$ gives $z=3/2-2w+w^2/2$. Writing $w=a+bi$, [F4] gives $r^2=a^2+b^2$ and hence $\operatorname{Re}(w^2)=a^2-b^2=2a^2-r^2$; therefore $\operatorname{Re}z=(1-a)^2+(1-r^2)/2$.

If $|\zeta|>1$, then $r<1$ and step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Re}z>0$. If $|\zeta|=1$, then $r=1$, so $\operatorname{Re}z=(1-a)^2\ge0$; equality forces $a=1$. Writing $w=1+bi$, [F4] gives $1=r^2=1+b^2$, so $b=0$ and $w=1$, hence $\zeta=1$ and $z=0$. This proves both assertions.

derivations.claim: Set $z=h\lambda=-h\rho+ih\omega$. Then $|1+z|^2=(1-h\rho)^2+(h\omega)^2=1-2h\rho+h^2(\rho^2+\omega^2)$.
By [F1], stability is equivalent to the last expression being at most one. Since $h>0$ and $\rho^2+\omega^2>0$, this is equivalent to $h(\rho^2+\omega^2)\le2\rho$, or $h\le2\rho/(\rho^2+\omega^2)$.

For forward Euler applied to $y'=\lambda y$, let $z=h\lambda$. Its stability function is $R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z$, and its absolute-stability region is exactly the closed disk

$$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z+1|\le1\}.$$

On the negative real axis, for $y'=-\rho y$ with $\rho>0$, the method is absolutely stable exactly when $0<h\rho\le2$.

citations.quote:
For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

Backward Euler on $y'=\lambda y$ is the scalar update $y_{n+1}=y_n+z y_{n+1}$, where $z=h\lambda$. Its stability function is

$$R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z)=\frac{1}{1-z}.$$

It is A-stable and L-stable.

The trapezoidal rule on $y'=\lambda y$ is

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+\frac z2(y_n+y_{n+1}),\qquad z=h\lambda.$$

Its stability function is $R_{\mathrm T}(z)=(1+z/2)/(1-z/2)$. It is A-stable but not L-stable.

For $\operatorname{Re}z\le0$, let $\zeta$ be any root of the constant-step BDF2 test polynomial $P_z(\zeta)=(3-2z)\zeta^2-4\zeta+1$. As $|z|\to\infty$ within the closed left half-plane, every such root satisfies $\zeta\to0$.

This is a multistep damping statement. It does not extend the one-step definition of L-stability to multistep methods.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: The function $u(t)=\exp(-\rho t)$ is continuous on $[0,h]$ by [F13], has $u(0)=1$ by [F1], and satisfies $u\prime(t)=-\rho\exp(-\rho t)=-\rho u(t)$ on $(0,h)$ by [F2], [F3], and [F12]. Thus it is a classical solution.

Let $y$ be any classical solution from the Given and set $v(t)=\exp(\rho t)y(t)$ on $[0,h]$. By [F13] and [F9], $v$ is continuous there. On $(0,h)$, [F8], [F2], [F3], and [F12] give $v\prime(t)=\rho\exp(\rho t)y(t)+\exp(\rho t)y\prime(t)=0$. So [F10] makes $v$ constant; since $v(0)=1$, [F11] gives $y(h)=1/\exp(\rho h)=\exp(-x)$. The exact one-step factor is therefore $\exp(-x)$.
At $z=-x$, [F5] gives $R_{\mathrm{BE}}(-x)=1/(1+x)\to0$, and [F6] gives $R_{\mathrm T}(-x)=(1-x/2)/(1+x/2)\to-1$.

Since $-x$ lies in the closed left half-plane, [F7] gives that both BDF2 roots tend to zero as $x\to\infty$. By [F4] and step 1.2 the exact factor also tends to zero. Therefore $|R_{\mathrm T}(-x)-\exp(-x)|\to1$, exhibiting the trapezoidal fast-mode damping defect without making a general accuracy claim.

No endpoint derivative, general accuracy bound, variable-grid damping, multistep L-stability or AC is asserted.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $G\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite. Define the inner product and its vector norm on $\mathbb R^d$ by

$$\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^\mathsf{T}Gy,\qquad \|x\|_G=\sqrt{x^\mathsf{T}Gx}.$$

For $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, its induced operator norm is $\|M\|_G=\sup_{x\ne0}\|Mx\|_G/\|x\|_G$. A matrix step $M$ is contractive in this specified inner product when $\|M\|_G\le1$.

For $A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, its logarithmic norm in the same inner product is

$$\mu_G(A)=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{x^\mathsf{T}GAx}{x^\mathsf{T}Gx}.$$

In the Euclidean inner product $G=I$, write $\|\cdot\|_2$ and $\mu_2$. A real matrix is normal when $AA^\mathsf{T}=A^\mathsf{T}A$ and nonnormal otherwise.

For a rational stability function $R=P/Q$, the matrix step $R(hA)$ is defined only when $Q(hA)$ is invertible; its contractivity is the separate condition $\|R(hA)\|_G\le1$.

Backward Euler on $y'=\lambda y$ is the scalar update $y_{n+1}=y_n+z y_{n+1}$, where $z=h\lambda$. Its stability function is

$$R_{\mathrm{BE}}(z)=\frac{1}{1-z}.$$

It is A-stable and L-stable.

derivations.claim: The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is $(\nu+1)^2$, so its roots are both $-1$ and the scalar backward-Euler factor is $R_{\mathrm{BE}}(-1)=1/2$. Also $A A^\mathsf{T}\ne A^\mathsf{T}A$, so $A$ is nonnormal.

Direct inversion gives $(I-A)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&4\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix}$. For $e_2=(0,1)^\mathsf{T}$, this step gives $(4,1/2)^\mathsf{T}$, whose Euclidean norm is $\sqrt{65/4}>1=\|e_2\|_2$. Thus the matrix step is not contractive.

For $x=(x_1,x_2)^\mathsf{T}$, $7\|x\|_2^2-x^\mathsf{T}Ax=8(x_1-x_2)^2\ge0$, with equality at $x_1=x_2\ne0$. Hence $\mu_2(A)=7>0$, which records the nonnormal growth hidden by the negative scalar test value. The claimed implication is false.

The Statement refuted is a universal implication from left-half-plane scalar spectrum to Euclidean backward-Euler contractivity, not a biconditional.
The counterexample disproves that one-way implication; it does not assert or investigate its converse, and the explicit nonnormal witness remains the whole claim.
